v0.6.0 gave fufu a verb for sending work out of the machine. Using it on a real repository turned up the thing underneath: fufu could see a remote perfectly well and would not say so. It guessed the name was origin, left what the remotes hold off the screen entirely, called the net healthy while both wire verbs were dead, and refused to let a base live anywhere but locally. This release is that whole seam.

**The remote stops being a guess**

`ff remote` is the verb that answers "which names are there?". Every refusal that said "no remote named upstream" owed the reader that list, and until now the way to get it was `ff git remote -v` — fufu handing you back to the tool it replaces, at the exact moment you were stuck. It reads through the ordinary repository handle, so a listing is never the reason fufu reaches outside its own process.

`ff branch list` grows a third bucket. fufu could walk `refs/remotes/` the whole time and simply never showed you: a clone with a dozen branches on the remote listed the one you were standing on. Rows under `remote only:` are the tracking refs no local branch already stands on — subtracted by ref rather than by name, because a branch's name is the wrong axis for that question — newest first, bounded at ten with `--all` and a count row saying what the bound left out.

`ff publish --to <remote>` sends a branch to a named remote and records that it answers to it. Nothing in fufu had ever written `branch.<name>.remote`; the only thing that created an upstream was `git push -u` spawned from inside a push, so a repository with several remotes and none named origin was simply stuck — `ff sync` and `ff publish` both refused, and both exits pointed at raw git. Because the whole remote axis is derived from those two config keys, that single write un-refuses sync, gives status a remote to speak about, and gives doctor something to find. A `--to` naming a *different* remote than the branch already tracks is refused rather than obeyed, because the published-tip ref is keyed by branch and a silent retarget would offer the next lease against a tip the new remote never held.

And `branch/not-found` stops guessing. Its exit read `ff start origin/<branch>`, which is right only when the remote is called origin — in any other repository the error's own advice failed on the next line, which is worse than advice it never gave.

**Status and doctor stop being blind to it**

`ff status` said "nothing to sync" on branches where `ff sync` refuses to run, and `ff doctor` called the net sound while both wire verbs were dead — sixteen rows, every one ok or info, and the word *remote* appearing nowhere in the file.

The defect underneath was one line of type. A missing remote axis was doing two jobs: *this branch has no remote, and that is fine*, and *there is something to say and fufu declined to guess*. The second is exactly the state sync refuses on. The naming rule is a value now rather than a decision buried in a refusal, so status appends `remote unnamed` beside the `remote is gone` it already knew how to say, and doctor gains three rows: a branch answering to no nameable remote, config sections naming branches that are not here, and branches here whose shared copy has gone. The orphan row is graded by whether the tracking ref survives, because otherwise every ordinary published-delete would leave doctor complaining about something fufu did on purpose.

**`ff branch delete` says what it leaves behind**

Deleting a branch reported "deleted", promised `ff undo` puts it back, and silently left the tracking ref, both config keys, the published-tip ref, and the branch on the remote. With remote branches now on screen the deleted branch came back on the very next listing, which reads as the delete having failed.

So the report names the shared copy, and `ff branch delete <name> --shared` removes it too — one act in your head, one verb, since you cannot stand on the branch you are deleting. Local first, then the wire: a failed push leaves the local delete done and undoable and the copy intact. The cleanup follows the wire and nothing else, because none of those refs is tracked, so removing them on a plain delete would hand back a branch that lost its remote axis on an operation that is supposed to be exactly reversible.

**The fetch speaks the protocol itself**

`ff sync` no longer spawns `git fetch`. It negotiates and takes the pack in this process, over the same transport `ff clone` has been using.

Native here is a claim about the protocol and the porcelain, not about the process table, and that distinction is written down rather than glossed. Over http(s) the whole conversation is fufu's. A filesystem remote still spawns `git-upload-pack`, because that is what a local transport *is*, and an ssh URL still spawns `ssh`. The wire's repository handle deliberately reads the installation config, which costs one spawn per fetch and buys `insteadOf`, `http.proxy` and `credential.helper` — without it a fetch would look native and fail for exactly the people the old spawn was protecting.

The push stays spawned, and not for want of trust: the library speaks the half of the protocol that receives a pack and nothing that sends one. That is a fact about the dependency rather than a decision, so `sync/no-git` — "git is not on PATH, and fufu still spawns it" — became `publish/no-git`, which is the only place it was ever true.

**A base is a branch wherever it lives**

`ff start origin/feature` forked at the right commit, reported a bare sha, and recorded no parent at all — so a branch started from someone else's work had no base: status never said it moved, and sync lined it up against trunk instead. Remote parents are real now, resolved by ref and displayed by name, the way trunk already is.

`ff restack --onto origin/main` refused, and the reason it gave was a namespace. What that rule was actually protecting is one invariant, and it is not about namespaces: the base axis and the remote axis must never aim at the same ref, or a branch would answer to itself. So the stand-in is gone and the real test replaces it — a local name still wins, a local ambiguity stays an ambiguity rather than falling through to a remote guess, and `origin/main` and `refs/remotes/origin/main` are two spellings of one base.

What remains is a refusal owed to a person rather than to the code: aiming a branch at its own shared copy is reconciling with the remote, which is `ff sync`, and the exits say so. But sync's remote axis aims at that exact ref on purpose, and a resumed hold may be one — so the refusal knows whether a person typed it or machinery settled it, and only the first is refused.

`ff restack --onto origin/HEAD` reports a branch it cannot find, rather than an error about symbolic refs. Every clone leaves that ref behind and it is the one shape this path was guaranteed to meet.

**Smaller things**

`ff describe -b <new>` renamed everything about a branch except the one thing git itself carries. The renamed branch lost its remote axis, the stale config section was left naming a branch that no longer existed, and the next publish opened a *second* shared copy under the new name. On that one axis fufu was worse than the `git branch -m` it advertises itself as improving on; the section moves with the rename now, `merge` riding across verbatim because it names the branch on the remote side, which a local rename did not touch.

One table decides which ambient lanes ride an invocation. The pre-command snapshot, the daily auto-trim and the passive update check were hand-wired at individual call sites, and most sites were never written — four verbs captured nowhere, and the update lane fired from two places. It is exhaustive now, so a verb added without deciding its lanes is a compile error rather than a lane that silently never fires.

`ff -v` goes through the version verb. It was the argument parser's own version action, printing and exiting before any lane could run — a machine sat on a cached `latest` for hours while running the older build, because the only thing being typed was `--version`. One answer with two spellings, and it takes `--json`.

The README's console blocks are real output. Every one was captured from a single end-to-end run against a live bare remote, which is also what turned up two bugs in `ff start`: the park line named the fork source instead of the branch the change was on, and one line in the README described a fetch `ff start` has never performed.

**Numbers**

11 commits of product change over v0.6.0, +3,826/−376 across 61 files. 1,252 workspace tests, up from 1,191. 101 `ff explain` ids, up from 96.

The tag carries four more commits that change nothing you can run: CI now shards the Windows leg four ways, which took the pipeline from 19m48s to under 8 minutes. That number came out of measuring the runners rather than guessing at them — process creation costs 0.59ms on Linux and 6.6ms on Windows, real Windows hardware pays the same 6.6ms, and disk and memory were both ruled out with numbers. The one thing it gave up is finding a release-profile break before the tag rather than during it, since the fat-LTO build now happens once on Linux instead of on all three platforms.
